# Declock {#declock .hiddenheading}

My website provides many examples of the [Quarto](https://quarto.org) publishing and the [Dec](/dec) measurement systems in action. I leverage Quarto support for the [Observable](https://observablehq.com/) data analysis and visualization system to create animated and interactive graphics like the [bar📊charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_chart) clocks🕓, [solar☀️terminator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminator_%28solar%29#:~:text=a%20moving%20line%20that%20divides%20the%20daylit%20side%20and%20the%20dark%20night%20side%20of%20a%20planetary%20body) map🗺, [Earth🌍orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_orbit) diagram, and [daylight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight#:~:text=the%20combination%20of%20all%20direct%20and%20indirect%20sunlight%20during%20the%20daytime) [area chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_chart#:~:text=The%20area%20between%20axis%20and%20line%20are%20commonly%20emphasized%20with%20colors) below.

::: {.column-margin .clocks #onlymargin .posneg}
\${posclock}\${negclock}
:::

Dec times are measured in [fractional days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#Fractional_days:~:text=a%20decimal%20fraction%20of%20a%20day), often using [metric prefixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_prefix#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20that%20precedes%20a%20basic%20unit%20of%20measure%20to%20indicate%20a%20multiple%20or%20submultiple%20of%20the%20unit) like [deci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deci-#:~:text=a%20decimal%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20tenth), [centi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centi-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20hundredth), or [milli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milli-#:~:text=a%20unit%20prefix%20in%20the%20metric%20system%20denoting%20a%20factor%20of%20one%20thousandth). The top, middle, and bottom bars indicate the [decidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#:~:text=dividing%20the%20day%20into%2010%20decidays){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"}, [millidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_time#:~:text=1.44%20minutes%2C%20or%2086.4%20seconds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a day"}, and [centimillidays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#:~:text=which%20would%20be-,1/100%2C000%20day,-%2C%20or%20864%20milliseconds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundred thousandths of a day"}, respectively, of the time since the start, [+\${decTime}]{.point1}, or until the end, [-\${decTimeN}]{.point0}, of the day in the Dec [time zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone#:~:text=an%20area%20which%20observes%20a%20uniform%20standard%20time), \${decZoneHsl}, at the location of the red⭕️circle on the map beneath the bars.

To rotate the globe🌐in the Earth🌏orbit diagram, drag the red circle horizontally↔️or slide the red🔴dot on the daylight area chart vertically↕. The red circle's vertical position determines the yearly daylight pattern visualized by the area chart. Shift the vertical red<font color=red>—</font>line on the area chart horizontally to move the globe along the ellipse of the Earth🌎orbit.

{{< include /dec/time/_timecharts.qmd >}}

# Annual day aggregate (ada) {#sec-ada .hiddenheading}

The red line indicates a "day of year" ([doy](#doy){#dayofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}): \${selDateHsl}, which identifies a day in a year like a [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) month and "day of month" ([dom](#dom){#dayofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}). The red dot denotes a "time of day" ([tod](#tod){#timeofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}): \${selTimeDay}, which specifies a point in a day like an "hour minute second" ([hms](#hms){#hourminutesecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"}) triplet. Together, a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can form an "annual day aggregate" ([ada](#ada){#annualdayaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}): \${selDateHsl1} + \${selTimeDay1} &div; 1000 = \${selDateHsl2}.\${selTimeDay2}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup00}
$$
\begin{split}
\text{doy} &= \lfloor\text{ada}\rfloor \\
&= \text{ada} - \text{tod}
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-ada}
:::

As their names suggest, [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} and [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"} are measured in days. The [measurement unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_measurement#:~:text=a%20definite%20magnitude%20of%20a%20quantity) of a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can be a day or a [submultiple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_%28mathematics%29#Submultiple:~:text=of%20%22a%20being-,a%20unit%20fraction,-of%20b%22%20) of a day with a metric prefix. By changing how a decimal [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is measured, we can shift its [decimal separator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_separator#:~:text=a%20symbol%20that%20separates%20the%20integer%20part%20from%20the%20fractional%20part%20of%20a%20number) or turn it into an integer. The [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} along the y-axis of the area chart are integers because they have three digits and are measured in [millidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a day"}.

# Epochal day aggregate (eda) {#sec-eda .hiddenheading}

To obtain a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}, we can [keep the remainder after dividing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) by one to isolate the [decimal part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_part#:~:text=the%20excess%20beyond%20that%20number%27s%20integer%20part) of the [quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotient#:~:text=a%20quantity%20produced%20by%20the%20division%20of%20two%20numbers): \${zeroDotyHsl}.\${zeroTimeHsl0} [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 = [0]{.color0}.\${zeroTimeHsl1}. We can use this same approach to separate a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from an "epochal day aggregate" ([eda](#eda){#epochaldayaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"}): \${zeroDoteHsl}.\${zeroTimeHsl2} mod 1 = [0]{.color0}.\${zeroTimeHsl3}. The current [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"} tells us how many days have passed since the Dec [epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoch#:~:text=an%20instant%20in%20time%20chosen%20as%20the%20origin%20of%20a%20particular%20calendar%20era): Year [0]{.color0} Day [0]{.color0} [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [0]{.color0}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup01}
$$\begin{split}
\text{tod} &= \text{ada} \bmod 1 \\
&= \text{eda} \bmod 1
\end{split}$$ {#eq-tod}
:::

## UNIX time equation {#sec-ute .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

Similarly, [UNIX time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=the%20number%20of%20non%2Dleap%20seconds%20that%20have%20elapsed%20since%2000%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970%2C%20the%20Unix%20epoch) tallies the seconds since the [UNIX epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time#:~:text=00%3A00%3A00%20UTC%20on%201%C2%A0January%201970), which is exactly 719468 days after the Dec epoch. To get the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in Zone [0]{.color0}, the Dec time zone that is in between the two leftmost vertical lines on the map, we can divide UNIX time by the [number of seconds in a day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#:~:text=average%2C%20this%20is-,24%20hours%20(86%2C400%20seconds),-.%20As%20a%20day) and then keep the remainder after dividing the resulting days by 1 as in @eq-unixtod.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup02}
$$\text{tod} = \text{unix} \div 86400 \bmod 1$$ {#eq-unixtod}
:::

## Julian date equation {#sec-jde .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

[Julian dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=the%20Julian%20day%20number%20plus%20the%20fraction%20of%20a%20day%20since%20the%20preceding%20noon) track the days since the beginning of the [Julian period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=a%20chronological%20interval%20of%207980%C2%A0years%2C%20derived%20from%20three%20multi%2Dyear%20cycles:%20the%20Indiction%2C%20Solar%2C%20and%20Lunar%20cycles) and thus are akin to [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregates"}. We can produce a Zone [5]{.color5} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [Julian date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#:~:text=the%20Julian%20day%20number%20plus%20the%20fraction%20of%20a%20day%20since%20the%20preceding%20noon) simply by keeping the remainder after dividing by one. If we want a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} instead, we should add [5]{.color5} [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to the Julian date, divide the sum by one, and then keep the remainder as in @eq-juliantod below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup03}
$$\text{tod} = (\text{julian} + 0.5) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-juliantod}
:::

# Hour minute second {#sec-hms .hiddenheading}

We can also obtain a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [Coordinated Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time#:~:text=the%20primary%20time%20standard%20globally%20used%20to%20regulate%20clocks%20and%20time) ([UTC](#utc){#coordinateduniversaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet by summing its components after converting them to fractional days, as shown in the equation below. The [computer programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programming#:~:text=the%20composition%20of%20sequences%20of%20instructions%2C%20called%20programs%2C%20that%20computers%20can%20follow%20to%20perform%20tasks) code in the [tabset panel](https://quarto.org/docs/interactive/layout.html#tabset-panel) beneath the equation compares [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} derived from [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} and UNIX time as Quarto was [rendering](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/rstudio.html#rendering:~:text=When%20rendering%2C%20Quarto%20generates%20a%20new%20file%20that%20contains%20selected%20text%2C%20code%2C%20and%20results) this webpage.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup04}
$$\text{tod} = \dfrac{\text{hour}}{24} + \dfrac{\text{minute}}{1440} + \dfrac{\text{second}}{86400}$$ {#eq-hmstod}
:::

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
using Dates
hms = now(UTC)
hour(hms) / 24 +
minute(hms) / 1440 +
second(hms) / 86400 +
millisecond(hms) / 864e5
datetime2unix(hms) / 86400 % 1
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
hms = new Date();
hms.getUTCHours() / 24 +
hms.getUTCMinutes() / 1440 +
hms.getUTCSeconds() / 86400 +
hms.getUTCMilliseconds() / 864e5;
hms.getTime() / 864e5 % 1;
```

### Python

```{python}
from datetime import datetime, timezone
hms = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
hms.hour / 24 + \
hms.minute / 1440 + \
hms.second / 86400 + \
hms.microsecond / 864e8
hms.timestamp() / 86400 % 1
```

### R

```{r}
hms <- as.POSIXlt(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC")
hms$hour / 24 +
hms$min / 1440 +
hms$sec / 86400
(as.numeric(as.POSIXct(hms)) / 86400) %% 1
```

:::

Equations -@eq-dsa to -@eq-som below convert UNIX time or a Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into the three components of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet: the "hour of day" ([hod](#hod){#hourofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"}), "minute of hour" ([moh](#moh){#minuteofhour .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="minute of hour"}), and "second of minute" ([som](#som){#secondofminute .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second of minute"}), using a "daily second aggregate" ([dsa](#dsa){#dailysecondaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daily second aggregate"}) and "hourly second aggregate" ([hsa](#hsa){#hourlysecondaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hourly second aggregate"}). While both count seconds, [dsa](#dsa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daily second aggregates"} start at midnight ([Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [0]{.color0}) and [hsa](#hsa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hourly second aggregates"} begin at the [top of the hour](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/top_of_the_hour).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup05}
$$\begin{split}
\text{dsa} & = \text{tod} \ast 86400 \\
& = \text{unix} \bmod  86400
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-dsa}
$$
\text{hsa} = \text{dsa} \bmod  3600
$$ {#eq-hsa}
$$
\text{hod} = \lfloor \text{dsa} \div 3600 \rfloor
$$ {#eq-hod}
$$
\text{moh} = \lfloor \text{hsa} \div 60 \rfloor
$$ {#eq-moh}
$$
\text{som} = \lfloor \text{hsa} \bmod  60 \rfloor
$$ {#eq-som}
:::


:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
using Dates
dsa = datetime2unix(now(UTC)) / 86400 % 1 * 86400
hsa = dsa % 3600
map(x -> floor(Int, x), (dsa / 3600, hsa / 60, hsa % 60))
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
dsa = Date.now() / 864e5 % 1 * 86400;
hsa = dsa % 3600;
[dsa / 3600, hsa / 60, hsa % 60].map(Math.floor)
```

### Python

```{python}
from datetime import datetime, timezone
dsa = datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp() / 86400 % 1 * 86400
hsa = dsa % 3600
tuple(map(int, [dsa // 3600, hsa // 60, hsa % 60 // 1]))
```

### R

```{r}
dsa <- (as.numeric(as.POSIXct(Sys.time())) / 86400) %% 1 * 86400
hsa <- dsa %% 3600
sapply(c(dsa %/% 3600, hsa %/% 60, hsa %% 60), as.integer)
```

:::

# Universal time offset {#sec-uto .hiddenheading}

The [Global Positioning System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System#:~:text=a%20satellite%2Dbased%20hyperbolic%20navigation%20system), [BeiDou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BeiDou#:~:text=a%20satellite%2Dbased%20radio%20navigation%20system), and [Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_(satellite_navigation)#:~:text=a%20global%20navigation%20satellite%20system%20(GNSS)%20created%20by%20the%20European%20Union) [global navigation satellite systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_navigation#:~:text=a%20satellite%20navigation%20system%20with%20global%20coverage) along with most --- if not all --- [programming languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_language#:~:text=a%20system%20of%20notation%20for%20writing%20source%20code%20such%20as%20used%20to%20produce%20a%20computer%20program) do not account for [leap seconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=one%2Dsecond%20adjustment), which appears to be for the best given that leap seconds [can cause problems](https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/leap-seconds-faqs#:~:text=detriments%20to%20adding%20leap%20seconds) and will be abolished no later than [2027]{.color27by100}+[081]{.color081by366} according to the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures#:~:text=an%20intergovernmental%20organisation%20(IGO)%2C%20through%20which%20its%2067%20member%2Dstates%20act%20on%20measurement%20standards).

On or before the deadline to abolish leap seconds, the tolerance for disagreement between [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} and [Universal Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Time#Versions:~:text=a%20time%20standard%20based%20on%20Earth%27s%20rotation) ([UT](#ut){#universaltime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"}) will increase from [1 Dec second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=to%20ensure%20that%20the%20difference%20between%20the%20UTC%20and%20UT1%20readings%20will%20never%20exceed%200.9%20seconds) ([s](#s){#second .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}) to 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}. Since [1972]{.color72by100}+[122]{.color122by365}, only [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=27%20leap%20seconds%20have%20been%20added%20to%20UTC) leap seconds have been inserted, which is 0.75% of 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, and at this rate it will take over five millennia for the disparity between [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} and [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to reach 3750 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}.

Instead of leap seconds, Dec matches [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} using a "[universal time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Time#:~:text=a%20time%20standard%20based%20on%20Earth%27s%20rotation) [offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC_offset#:~:text=the%20difference%20in%20hours%20and%20minutes%20between%20Coordinated%20Universal%20Time%20(UTC)%20and%20the%20standard%20time%20at%20a%20particular%20place)" ([uto](#uto){#universaltimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"}). With the [leap second insertion dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second#:~:text=Announced%20leap%20seconds%20to%20date) provided by the [International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Earth_Rotation_and_Reference_Systems_Service#:~:text=the%20body%20responsible%20for%20maintaining%20global%20time%20and%20reference%20frame%20standards), we can approximate the [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"} that yields [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"} when added to the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} on the [Dec date](/dec/date) chosen by the [range](https://observablehq.com/framework/inputs/range)🎚️inputs below: \${leapCountHsl} &div; 8640 = \${leapSdecHsl}\${leapSb24hsl} &div; 90000 = \${leapTzoHsl0}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: dateinput
//| class: slider
viewof leapSecondYear = Inputs.range([1970, 2020], {label: "Year", value: 1995, step: 1})
viewof leapSecondDate = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day", value: 182, step: 1})
```

# Second interval difference {#sec-sid .hiddenheading}

The equation above divides leap seconds by the number of [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#:~:text=the%20world%27s%20most%20widely%20used%20system%20of%20measurement) ([SI](#si){#internationalsystemofunits .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"}) seconds ([sis](#sis){#sisecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"}) or Dec [deciseconds]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a second"} ([ds](#ds){#decisecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}) in a [deciday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a day"} ([dd](#dd){#deciday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"}): 8640 [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} = 90000 [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"} = 1 [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"}. To avoid [repeating decimals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=the%20same%20sequence%20of%20digits%20is%20repeated%20forever) when turning [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} into [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}, we can put a Dec [quadravigesimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#:~:text=24-,Quadravigesimal,-%5B48%5D) ([base24]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadravigesimal"}) digit in place of the ones digit and decimal part of the [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}: \${leapSdecHsl1}\${leapSb24hsl1} = \${leapSdecHsl2} &times; 10 + \${leapSsidHsl} &div; 2.4.

Known as a "second interval difference" ([sid](#sid){#secondintervaldifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval difference"}), the [base24]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadravigesimal"} ([b24](#b24){#base24 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}) character at the end of \${leapSdecHsl3}\${leapSb24hsl2} is a letter of the [Greek alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_alphabet#:~:text=the%20writing%20system%20used%20for%20the%20Greek%20language). To display [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} in [ds](#ds){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec deciseconds"}, we can concatenate the integer part of the [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} we obtain from @eq-sis with the [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} representation of the [sid](#sid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval difference"} we get from @eq-sid. The table beneath these equations lists [base10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal#:~:text=a%20numeral%20system%20that%20uses%20ten%20as%20its%20radix%20%28base%29) ([b10](#b10){#base10 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}) and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} equivalents.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup06}
$$
\text{s} = \dfrac{\text{ds}}{10} = \dfrac{\text{sis}}{0.96}
$$ {#eq-sis}
$$
\begin{split}
\text{sid} &= \text{sis} \bmod 24\\
&= (\text{s} - \text{sis}) \ast 24 \bmod 24
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-sid}
:::

## Base9 {#sec-b9 .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

Whereas [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} is like glue that allows us to combine [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} and [sid](#sid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval differences"}, Dec [nonary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_numeral_system#Compact_ternary_representation:_base_9_and_27:~:text=base%209%2C%20each%20digit%20is%20two%20ternary%20digits) ([base9]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="nonary"}) enables us to append [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. The table below shows the [astronomical symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_symbol#:~:text=symbols%20used%20to%20represent%20astronomical%20objects) used by Dec for [base9]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="nonary"} ([b9](#b9){#base9 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}). When we replace the "decimilliday" ([dmd](#dmd){#decimilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"}) digit in a [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with a [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit, the [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit counts tens of [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} instead of [dmd](#dmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"} and the next digit tracks [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} instead of "centimillidays" ([cmd](#cmd){#centimilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}).

A [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with four [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, one [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, and one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit can match the time represented by any [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet, because the product of the bases of its digits is evenly divisible by the number of [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} in a day: 10000 &times; 9 &times; 24 &div; 86400 = 216000 &div; 86400 = 25. For [hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"}, one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit is sufficient. The [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet selected by the range inputs below corresponds to [Hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"} \${b24hodHsl} and [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} \${hmsTodHsl}\${hmsSecHsl}\${hmsSidHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: hmsinput
//| class: slider
viewof hmsinput = Inputs.form([
  Inputs.range([0, 23], {label: "Hour", value: 11, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Minute", value: 0, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Second", value: 0, step: 1}),
])
```

## Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) {#sec-utc .hiddenheading}

There are 12 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that become a [terminating decimals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=a%20finite%20number%20of%20nonzero%20digits) in [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} after being converted from hours to days and therefore could be displayed in either [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} or [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Although it has only ten time zones, Dec can match the time in any [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with one or two non-negative [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. There are 27 UTC offsets that require only one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit and 11 that need two [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits.

Out of the [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets) [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, 14 are negative (&lt;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) and 24 are non-negative (&ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}). The [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with [the most negative offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9212:00#:~:text=a%20nautical%20time%20zone%20comprising%20the%20high%20seas%20between%20180%C2%B0%20and%20172%C2%B030%E2%80%B2W%20longitude) is completely uninhabited. The bar chart below visualizes [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) data from 2020 regarding the population of each [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone. The vast majority of all people live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with &ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets.

{{< include /dec/time/_tzpopplot.qmd >}}

Negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets only exist in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas#:~:text=a%20landmass%20comprising%20the%20totality%20of%20North%20America%20and%20South%20America) and islands in the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Atlantic_Ocean) and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean) Oceans. Therefore, the bar chart above is essentially comparing the populations of the Americas and the rest of the world. According to 2021 [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs#:~:text=part%20of%20the%20United%20Nations%20Secretariat) data, about one billion out of a total of almost eight billion people live in the Americas.

Dec forbids the association of dates with negative offsets. Therefore, Dec will add ten [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to any negative offset and add one day to the date associated with that offset. Negative offset handling has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or the conversion of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and is typically only necessary after a "year month day" ([ymd](#ymd){#yearmonthday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"}) triplet is converted into a Dec date.

If we do know whether Day [364]{.color364by365} belongs to a common or leap year, adding one day to it yields either Day [0]{.color0} or Day [365]{.color365by366} and this uncertainty is expressed as a [multiplication sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication_sign) over the last digit of [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0}. The sign hints that [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is short for [365]{.color0}&times;`leap`, where [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is either [365]{.color365by366} if `leap` is 1 or [0]{.color0} if `leap` is 0. We can find `leap` by passing any year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}) to @eq-leap below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07}
$$
\text{leap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 100\neq0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-leap}

:::

# Day of week {#sec-dow .hiddenheading}

Adding one day to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, but it increments the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} and "day of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). Dec meets the expectations of [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20currently%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) users who live in UTC time zones with negative offsets by essentially deriving the previous [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} or [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} from the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} if a location in the Americas is provided without an offset or with a negative offset.

# Time zone offset {#sec-tzo .hiddenheading}

In Dec, "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) are derived solely from longitude. Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}), arcbeats ([a](#a){#arcbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}), or submultiples thereof. If we travel East or West until we reach our starting point, we will cover 1 [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal line on a map"} or 100000 ([10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"}) [a](#a){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}. A [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} is essentially a [deciwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a wěi"} ([dw](#dw){#deciwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}) longitude that became a single-digit [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} integer via  [truncation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncation#Truncation_and_floor_function:~:text=truncation%20is%20limiting%20the%20number%20of%20digits%20right%20of%20the%20decimal%20point) or [flooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=takes%20as%20input%20a%20real%20number%20x%2C%20and%20gives%20as%20output%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x): &LeftFloor;\${longInputHsl} &div; 100&RightFloor; = \${longFloorHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput
//| class: slider
viewof lonInput = Inputs.range([0, 999], {label: "Milliwěi", value: 500, step: 1})
```

The [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is approximately ([~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}) 1 [taur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="circumference = 𝜏r"} ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="a hundred thousand"} [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) long. Near the Equator, a longitude that has a [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_degrees#Precision) of 0.1 [microwěi]{#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of wěi"} ([&micro;w](#uw){#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microwěi"}) or 10 milliarcbeats ([ma](#ma){#milliarcbeats .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}) is accurate to within [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.1 [microtaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of taur"} ([&micro;c](#uc){#microtaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microtaur"}), [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}10 "zone equatorial meters" ([zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), or 4 [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre#Definition:~:text=the%20base%20unit%20of%20length%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units), which is about the width of a [U-shaped living room layout](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/living-room-layouts) or the length of a typical [subcompact car](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/subcompact-cars-b-segment).

For precise [geopositioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopositioning#:~:text=estimating%20the%20geographic%20position%20of%20an%20object%20or%20a%20person), we may want to express [geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) in [ma](#ma){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}, but we are unlikely to need [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} when displaying the [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) or estimates of what the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will be when the Sun rises, reaches its [highest point of the day](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon), or sets. By default, Dec uses [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} precision to display a solar time and the "solar time offset" ([sto](#sto){#solartimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}) used to produce it.

# Equation of time {#sec-eot .hiddenheading}

The two types of [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) are ["mean solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Mean_solar_time:~:text=it%20follows%20an%20imaginary%20%22mean%20Sun%22%20that%20moves%20along%20the%20celestial%20equator%20at%20a%20constant%20rate%20that%20matches%20the%20real%20Sun%27s%20average%20rate%20over%20the%20year) ([mst](#mst){#meansolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}) and ["apparent solar time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Apparent_solar_time:~:text=the%20apparent%20motion%20of%20the%20actual%20Sun) ([ast](#ast){#apparentsolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}). To calculate an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, we keep only the decimal part of the sum of 0.95, the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} measured in days, and a longitude measured in [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}. If we want [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} instead of [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}, the sum needs to include the result of plugging the "time of year" ([toy](#toy){#timeofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}) into the ["equation of time"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_time#:~:text=the%20discrepancy%20between%20two%20kinds%20of%20solar%20time) ([eot](#eot){#equationoftime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup08}
$$\text{syl} = \text{leap} + 365$$ {#eq-syl}

$$\text{toy} = \text{ada} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toy}

$$\text{mst} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-mst}

$$\text{ast} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w} +  \text{eot}) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-ast}
:::

To obtain a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}, we divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} by a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which is the number of days in the year. Dec passes the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} directly from @eq-toy to the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} function in @eq-eot without first multiplying it by 2𝜋 or 𝜏 to convert it from [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}) to [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}) because the [sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20side%20opposite%20that%20angle%20to%20the%20length%20of%20the%20longest%20side%20of%20the%20triangle) and [cos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20adjacent%20leg%20to%20that%20of%20the%20hypotenuse) [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions#:~:text=functions%20which%20relate%20an%20angle%20of%20a%20right%2Dangled%20triangle%20to%20ratios%20of%20two%20side%20lengths) used by Dec are designed for [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09}
$$\begin{split}
\text{eot} & = \beta_0 \\
& + \beta_1 \ast \text{cos(toy)} \\
& + \beta_2 \ast \text{sin(toy)} \\
& + \beta_3 \ast \text{cos(2} \ast \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_4 \ast \text{sin(2} \ast \text{toy)}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-eot}
:::

By comparing the `sincost` and `sincos` functions, the code below demonstrates that using [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} rather than [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} can [yield more accurate results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=Representing%20angles%20in%20turns%20or%20half%2Dturns%20has%20accuracy%20advantages). Whereas `sincost` expects to receive [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} and is always correct, `sincos` assumes that it will get [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} and generates the slightly incorrect [E notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_notation#E_notation) values below because it cannot produce zero unless its input is zero.

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
sincost(x) = sincospi(2 * x)
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
sincospi = require(
  'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/stdlib-js/math-base-special-sincospi@umd/browser.js'
  )
function sincost(x) {
  return sincospi(2 * x);
}
function sincos(x) {
  return [Math.sin(x), Math.cos(x)]
}
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(1 * 2 * Math.PI)
```

### Python

```{python}
from math import cos, sin, pi, cospi, sinpi

def sincost(x):
    x *= 2
    return sinpi(x), cospi(x)

def sincos(x):
    return sin(x), cos(x)

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### R

```{r}
sincost <- function(x) {
  x <- 2 * x
  c(sinpi(x), cospi(x))
}

sincos <- function(x) {
  c(sin(x), cos(x))
}

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

:::

The values below are the coefficients of a [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic#:~:text=positive%20integer%20multiple%20of%20the%20fundamental%20frequency) [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model#:~:text=embodies%20a%20set%20of%20statistical%20assumptions%20concerning%20the%20generation%20of%20sample%20data), adapted from the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.noaa.gov) ([NOAA](#noaa){#nationaloceanicandatmosphericadministration .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"}) [General Solar Position Calculations](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/solareqns.PDF). Before [fitting](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.curve_fit.html) the model to [NOAA](#noaa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"} [yearly solar data](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/calcdetails.html), Dec divides [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values by 1.44 to convert minutes to [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}, converts [ymd](#ymd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"} triplet dates and [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet times into [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"}, and sorts by [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

{{< embed eot.ipynb#eotcoef >}}

{{< include /dec/time/_eotplot.qmd >}}

In the [line📈chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_chart#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20chart%20that%20displays%20information%20as%20a%20series%20of%20data%20points%20called%20%27markers%27%20connected%20by%20straight%20line%20segments) above, the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values range from -9.8 to 11.4 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} and the range of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [-365]{.color0} to [365]{.color365by366}, represents a common year followed by a leap year. The [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} reaches about one [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredth of a day"} ([cd]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}) on Days [245]{.color245by365} and [349]{.color349by365}, but passes through zero on Days [45]{.color045by365}, [103]{.color103by365}, [184]{.color184by365}, and [299]{.color299by365}. Therefore, [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} are equivalent four times per year.

Apart from transforming an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} into an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, we can also use [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values to more accurately estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow), sunrise, and sunset. @eq-solarnoon below creates a [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow) [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by keeping only the decimal part of the result of subtracting a [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} longitude and an [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} value that is measured in days from the sum of 9.55 and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} that is measured in days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10}
$$\text{solarnoon} = \left(9.55 + \text{tzo} - \text{w} - \text{eot}\right) \bmod 1$$ {#eq-solarnoon}
:::

# Cambridge and Cambridge {#sec-cac .hiddenheading}

To compare the solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in two cities, we can plug the longitude of each city into @eq-solarnoon above. If all of the variables other than longitude in @eq-solarnoon are set to zero, the resulting solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is almost five [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge#:~:text=a%20city%20and%20non%2Dmetropolitan%20district%20in%20the%20county%20of%20Cambridgeshire%2C%20England) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom#:~:text=a%20country%20in%20Northwestern%20Europe) and nearly seven [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts#:~:text=a%20city%20in%20Middlesex%20County%2C%20Massachusetts%2C%20United%20States) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States#:~:text=a%20country%20primarily%20located%20in%20North%20America).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11}
$$4.99635 = (9.55 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk}

$$6.97517 = (9.55 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema}
:::

The two homonymous cities are about two [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} apart and therefore will always differ by around two [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} in solar time, regardless of what time zone we use as our frame of reference. England is in Zone [0]{.color0} and Massachusetts is in Zone [8]{.color8}. From the perspective of Zone [8]{.color8}, solar noon is roughly [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [5]{.color5} in Cambridge, MA and about [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [3]{.color3} in Cambridge, UK.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12}
$$2.99635 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.050365) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk8}

$$4.97517 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.852484) \bmod 1 \ast 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema8}
:::

# Light arc whole {#sec-law .hiddenheading}

The path in the sky that the Sun appears to follow from a sunrise to a sunset is a "light [arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_path#:~:text=arc%2Dlike%20path%20that%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20follow%20across%20the%20sky) whole" ([law](#law){#lightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}). Solar noon, the midpoint of a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}, is halfway between sunrise and sunset. A [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} can be evenly split into two "light arc halves" ([lah](#lah){#lightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"}). Whereas [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} are time points, [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc wholes"} and [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc halves"} are durations. The difference between a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} is a sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13}
$$\text{law} = \text{lah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-law}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunrise}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} \\
& = \text{sunset} - \text{law}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunrise}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunset}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{sunrise} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} + \text{lah} \\
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunset}
:::

## Night arc whole {#sec-naw .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

The Sun continues its path after it disappears below the horizon, moving from sunset to sunrise along a "night arc whole" ([naw](#naw){#nightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc"}). Like [conjugate angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=conjugate%20angles%20sum%20to%20a%20full%20angle), a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} form a full circle that represents one day. Likewise, a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} and a "night arc half" ([nah](#nah){#nightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc half"}) are like two [supplementary angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=sum%20to%20a%20straight%20angle) that form a semicircle from solar noon to the [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} midpoint: [solar midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight#:~:text=the%20time%20opposite%20to%20solar%20noon%2C%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20closest%20to%20the%20nadir%2C%20and%20the%20night%20is%20equidistant%20from%20dusk%20and%20dawn).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14}
$$\text{naw} = \text{nah} \ast 2$$ {#eq-naw}

$$\begin{split}
\text{day}
& = \text{law} + \text{naw} \\
& = (\text{lah} + \text{nah}) \ast 2
\end{split}$$ {#eq-day}

$$\begin{split}
\text{solarmidnight}
&= \text{sunrise} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{sunset} - \text{law} - \text{nah}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-solarmidnight}
:::

The range input below controls the yellow [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and the blue [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} in the diagram beneath it. At the Equator, the sun always rises about a quarter turn from North and sets around three quarter turns from North, resulting in a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of roughly half a day: 75% [-]{.mono} 25% = 50%. If the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is zero, a [polar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_night#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20below%20the%20horizon%20for%20more%20than%2024%C2%A0hours) occurs. A day without a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} is called a [polar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20visible%20at%20the%20local%20midnight).

{{< include /dec/time/_dayarcplot.qmd >}}

The numbers in the diagram above are ["solar azimuth angle"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_azimuth_angle#:~:text=horizontal%20angle%20with%20respect%20to%20north) ([saa](#saa){#solarazimuthangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} ([mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}). At solar noon, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is 0 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20%28hemisphere%29%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20south%20of%20the%20equator) and 500 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator). The [radio](https://observablehq.github.io/framework/inputs/radio#:~:text=allows%20the%20user%20to%20choose%20one%20of%20a%20given%20set%20of%20values)📻input above controls whether the midpoint of the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is 0 or 500 [mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}. To measure the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} during the [daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location), point a compass🧭at the spot on the horizon below the Sun.

During an [equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator) at the Equator, the Sun goes directly from East to West, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} flips like a switch from 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} to 0.75 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} at solar noon, the "[solar elevation angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_zenith_angle#Summary_of_special_angles:~:text=For%20example%2C%20the-,solar,-elevation%20angle%20is)" ([sea](#sea){#solarelevationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}) peaks at 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}, and solar time is 0.5 − sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) &times; (0.25 [−]{.mono} [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}). To obtain the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, we can use the height (h) of a vertical rod on a level surface and the length (L) of its shadow: [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} = atan2(h, L).

In addition to determining the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, the  [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) function can also be used to calculate solar time, as shown in @eq-solartime, where [j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is a latitude measured in [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}). In Dec, [inverse trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions#:~:text=obtain%20an%20angle%20from%20any%20of%20the%20angle%27s%20trigonometric%20ratios) functions such as [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) yield [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} rather than [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. At the Equator, the latitude is zero [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and the [right-hand side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sides_of_an_equation#:~:text=The%20expression%20on%20the%20right%20side%20of%20the%20%22%3D%22%20sign) of @eq-solartime simplies to 0.5 + atan2(-sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"})cos([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}), sin([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"})).

$$
\text{solartime} = 0.5 + \text{atan2}\left(
\begin{aligned}
& \text{-sin(saa)cos(sea),} \\
& \text{sin(sea)cos(j) } - \\
& \text{cos(saa)cos(sea)sin(j)}
\end{aligned}
\right)
$$ {#eq-solartime}

At the North Pole, the latitude is 0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and the right-hand side of @eq-solartime simplifies to [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. At the South Pole, the latitude is -0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and the right-hand side of @eq-solartime simplifies to 0.5 [−]{.mono} [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} if [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is less than or equal to 0.5 a. We can approximate solar time with [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} in the Northern Hemisphere and is roughly equal to the  to Southern Hemisphere. As we approach either one of the poles, the solar time approximation provided by [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} becomes more accurate. As we  solar time is exactly equal to the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. Likewise, solar time is approximately equal to Equator and the South Pole, solar time is 

Dec measures latitude in turns called  or submultiples thereof such as millijīng ([mj](#mj){#millijing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millijīng"}). [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is 0 and 
In the Northern Hemisphere, [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is above 0 and we can interpret the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} as the solar time. In the Southern Hemisphere [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is less than 0 and solar time the difference between 1.5 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} and [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}: solartime = 1.5 [-]{.mono} [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}.

The bar chart beneath @eq-solartime compares the populations of the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

The clockwise path that the Sun follows in the Northern Hemisphere is ingrained in the Belarussian, Polish, and Ukrainian languages. As shown in @tbl-slav, these three Slavic languages each have one word for north or midnight and another word for south or noon. In Dec, zero represents both north and midnight, while both south and noon can be expressed as a half turn.

::: {.overflowtable}
 | Turns | Direction | Time     | Belarussian | Polish   | Ukrainian |
 | ----- | --------- | -------- | ----------- | -------- | --------- |
 | 0     | north     | midnight | поўнач      | północ   | північ    |
 | 0.5   | south     | noon     | поўдзень    | południe | південь   |
::: {#tbl-slav}

If we only want to know how long the Sun will shine on a given day, we can use the top equation below to obtain a [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"}. Alternatively, if we are interested in finding out when the Sun will rise or set on a given day, we will need to calculate a [da/2](#da2){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="half day arc"} using the bottom equation below and then combine it with a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} to get a sunrise or sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.


::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15}
$$\text{da} = \dfrac{\arccos\left({\Large\dfrac{\text{costau(0.252314)} - \text{sintau(m)} \ast \text{sintau(sda)}}{\text{costau(m)} \ast \text{costau(sda)}}}\right)}{\pi}$$ {#eq-da}

$$\dfrac{\text{da}}{2} = \dfrac{\arccos\left({\Large\dfrac{\text{costau(0.252314)} - \text{sintau(m)} \ast \text{sintau(sda)}}{\text{costau(m)} \ast \text{costau(sda)}}}\right)}{\tau}$$ {#eq-halfda}
:::

## Solar declination angle {#sec-sda .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

The [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} and [da/2](#da2){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="half day arc"} equations above require a latitude and a "solar [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination#:~:text=one%20of%20the%20two%20angles%20that%20locate%20a%20point%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere%20in%20the%20equatorial%20coordinate%20system) angle" ([sda](#sda){#solardeclinationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}). For simplicity, we can fit our [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} model to [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} data instead of fitting the needlessly complex [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model provided by the NOAA General Solar Position Calculations:

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16}
$$\begin{split}
\text{sda(toy)} & = \beta_0 \\
& + \beta_1 \ast \text{costau(toy)} \\
& + \beta_2 \ast \text{sintau(toy)} \\
& + \beta_3 \ast \text{costau(2} \ast \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_4 \ast \text{sintau(2} \ast \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_5 \ast \text{costau(3} \ast \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_6 \ast \text{sintau(3} \ast \text{toy)} \\
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sda}
:::

The top range input below picks the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that will become the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} in our fitted [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model. The other two range inputs below chose the geographic coordinates that we need to find the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}. While the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} depend on both geographic coordinates, the [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} varies only by latitude and not by longitude: ${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} -- ${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: doyinput
//| class: slider
viewof doyInput = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day of year", value: 183, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: latinput
//| class: slider
viewof latInput = Inputs.range([-250, 250], {label: "Latitude", value: 0, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput1
//| class: slider
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 1000], {step: 1, label: "Longitude"}), viewof lonInput)
```

The equation controlled by range inputs above can be summarized as sunset -- sunrise = [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} and can be rearranged into the sunrise equation: sunrise = sunset -- [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"}. If we plug the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in place of the sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in the sunrise equation without changing the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, the [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} will be replaced with the time until or since sunset: ${selectedCurrent.toFixed(3)} = ${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} ${selectedDifference < 0 ? "--" : "+"} ${parseFloat(Math.abs(selectedDifference).toFixed(3))}.

The latest equation above is an example of a Dec span. From left to right, this span consists of a [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted), an equals sign (=), [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted), a plus (+) or a minus (--) sign, and a [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference). A minus sign indicates the difference is the time remaining **until** sunset, whereas a plus sign means that the difference is the time that has passed **since** sunset.

The difference shows the [remaining time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event) as a negative number if the minuend is less than the substrahend or displays the [elapsed time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Elapsed_Time) as a positive number if the minuend is greater than the subtrahend. In this way, the difference can act like a ["T minus countdown"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining) that becomes a ["T plus countup"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=After%20a%20launch%2C%20most%20countdown%20clocks%20begin%20to%20show%20Mission%20Elapsed%20Time) after an event like a rocket🚀launch.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17}
$$\begin{cases}\text{difference}<0&{\text{if } \text{minuend} < \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}=0&{\text{if minuend} = \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}>0&{\text{if minuend}>\text{subtrahend.}}\end{cases}$$ {#eq-difference}
:::

When the minuend is the current time and the subtrahend is the [timestamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timestamp#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20characters%20or%20encoded%20information%20identifying%20when%20a%20certain%20event%20occurred) of an event which occurred in the past, the difference is the time elapsed since that event. A Dec timestamp consists of a year, a day, . can be an [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"}, a "epochal year aggregate" ([eya](#eya){#epochalyearaggregate .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"}), or a snap🫰. Eda and eya are  the time The typical snap format is year[+]{.mono}[ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}[-]{.mono}[tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}. The snap \${loadYearHsl}[+]{.mono}\${loadAdaHsl}[-]{.mono}[0]{.color0} represents the [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beat"} when this webpage loaded ${elaTimeHsl} [b](#b){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"} ago.

# Epochal year aggregate (eya) {#sec-eya .hiddenheading}

A [doe](#doe){#dayofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} is essentially a Dec date with a [yoe](#yoe){#yearofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} that is always equal to 0 and a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that is [not restricted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_set#:~:text=a%20set%20which%20is%20not%20bounded) to 0 &le; [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} &le; 365. Similarly, a Dec "epochal year aggregate" ([eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"}) is basically a Dec date with a non-integer year and a day permanently set to [0]{.color0}. We can obtain a Dec date by passing a doe Both [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} and [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregates"} allow us to represent a date as a single number and obtain the difference between two dates.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18}
$$\text{cda} = \text{de} - \text{coe} \ast 146097$$ {#eq-cda}

$$\text{yoc} = \biggl \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc} - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{1460} \rfloor + \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{36524} \rfloor - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{146096} \rfloor}{365} \biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-yocdoc}

$$\text{yoe} = \text{yoc} + \text{coe} \ast 400$$ {#eq-yoe}

$$\text{doy} = \biggl \lfloor \text{doc} - \text{yoc} \ast 365 - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{yoc}}{4} \rfloor + \lfloor \dfrac{\text{yoc}}{100} \rfloor \biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-doydoc}
:::

Compared to a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"}, it is much easier to convert between an [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"} and a to turn into Dec dates. The decimal part of an [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"} is a called a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}. We can convert between dates to [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of year"} with the equations below. We can obtain a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} by flooring an [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"}. Likewise, we can obtain a [doy]{.cyan .under .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} by flooring the product of [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} and the decimal part of an [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"}, which is called a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}. The current [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"} equation values are \${fullfracYear} = \${decYear} + \${decDoty} &div; \${nDaysInYear}. We can floor an [eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"} to get a yoe or divide its , we can obtain a 

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup19}
$$\text{eya} = \text{yoe} + \text{toy} = \text{yoe} + \text{doy} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-eya}

$$\text{toy} = \text{eya} \bmod 1 = \text{doy} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toyeya}

$$\text{doy} = \lfloor\text{toy}\ast\text{syl}\rfloor$$ {#eq-doytoy}

$$\text{eya} = \text{yoe} + \text{doy} \ast \text{syl}$$ {#eq-eyadoy}

$$\text{eya} = \text{yoe} + \text{coe} \ast 400$$ {#eq-eyacoe}
:::

[eya](#eya){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal year aggregate"} = [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} + [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} &div; [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}. 

We can omit the year from a snap if we replace the [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} with a subtrahend and a difference or just a difference. If needed, we can obtain a snap from a difference using the equations below. First, we subtract the difference from the current [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"} to obtain the "[eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"} difference difference" ([edd](#edd){#edadifferencedifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="eda difference difference"}). Then, we use the [edd](#edd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="eda difference difference"} to get the "cycle of era" ([coe](#coe){#cycleofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cycle of era"}), "day of cycle" ([doc](#doc){#dayofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"}), "year of cycle" ([yoc](#yoc){#yearofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of cycle"}), and then finally the year and [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup20}
$$\text{edd} = \text{eda} - \text{difference}$$ {#eq-edd}

$$\text{coe} = \Biggl \lfloor \dfrac{\begin{cases}\text{edd}&{\text{if } \text{edd} \geq 0;}\\\text{edd}-146096&{\text{otherwise.}}\end{cases}}{146097} \Biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-coe}

$$\text{doc} = \text{edd} - \text{coe} \ast 146097$$ {#eq-doc}

$$\text{yoc} = \biggl \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc} - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{1460} \rfloor + \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{36524} \rfloor - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{doc}}{146096} \rfloor}{365} \biggr \rfloor$$ {#eq-yocedd}

$$\text{year} = \text{yoc} + \text{coe} \ast 400$$ {#eq-year}

$$\text{ada} = \text{doc} - \text{yoc} \ast 365 - \lfloor \dfrac{\text{yoc}}{4} \rfloor + \lfloor \dfrac{\text{yoc}}{100} \rfloor$$ {#eq-adadoc}
:::

In the equations above, [eda](#eda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="epochal day aggregate"} is "epochal day aggregate", [coe](#coe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cycle of era"} is "cycle of era", [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"} is "day of cycle", and [yoc](#yoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of cycle"} is "year of cycle".

We can omit the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} if the timestamp is based on Zone [0]{.color0}.
