If needed, calculate the year by subtracting the [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} and &Delta; from the current eda and passing the result to the equations below.


To make it easier to compare timestamps, we should agree to always set the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} to zero. If we use a non-zero [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}, we should include it in between the event time and the elapsed time.

Let’s say that you live in Zone [0]{.color0} and there are four [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} that are vital to your typical daily rhythm: you start work at [375]{.color375} md, take a lunch break from [525]{.color525} to [575]{.color575} md, and finish work at [725]{.color725} md. After one event passes, you can begin tracking the time until the next one and thus cycle through all four over the course of each day: current = [375]{.color375} diff = [525]{.color525} diff = [575]{.color575} diff = [725]{.color725} diff.

Tzo range input (include tzo only if not zero)

Another use case for minuend expansion is travel. If the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is the minuend and your estimated arrival time is the subtrahend, then travel time remaining will be the difference. When traveling, we can replace time with distance so that distance traveled so far is the minuend, the total distance is the subtrahend, and the distance remaining is the difference. Apart from travel, measuring distance in addition to time can be useful for tracking exercise such as running, bicycling, or swimming.

To measure distances, Dec uses taur ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or zem ([z](#z){#zoneequatorialmeter .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), with or without metric prefixes, depending on the order of magnitude of the distance being measured. One [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} is close to the circumference of the earth and is equal to 10^5^ kilozem ([kz](#kz){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) or 4 &times 10^5^ kilometers ([km](#km){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="kilometers"}). The distance between the Earth and the Moon ranges from 9.065 to 10.135 c. For larger distances, we can use astronomical units (au), light years (ly), or multiples of [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} such as kilotaur ([kc](#kc){#kilotaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="kilotaur"}) and gigataur ([gc](#gc){#gigataur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="gigataur"}).

au = 3740 c = 3.74 kc
ly ‎ =  236525000 c = 236525 kc = 2.36525 gc

Speed is distance over time. Dec measures speed in omegar ([v]{}).
The speed of the rotation of the Earth is close to one v and is equal to one c per day or one kz per b. The average speed of the orbit of the Moon around the Earth is about 2.2 v and the mean speed of the  Earth orbit around the Sun is approximately 64 v. For higher speeds, we can use percent (%) or permille (‰) light speed (ls) and multiples of v like kv.

%ls ‎ =  10‰ls ‎ =  647552 v = 647.552 kv

For distances that we can measure on Earth, we may want to use submultiples of c such as mc or nc. One mc is 100 kz or 40 km and one nc is 1 decizem (dz) or 4 centimeters (cm). Similarly, we can use  submultiples of v for speeds on Earth. One milliomegar (mv) is one mc per day, one kz per centiday (cd), or one z per b and is very close to one mile per hour. An airplane flying at an average speed of 500 mv will travel the 12500 kz from Cambridge MA to Cambridge UK in a quarter day: 12500 kz / 500 mv = 25 cd.

Around the world in 80 days is a book published by Jules Verne in 1872. The average speed of a trip around the circumference of the earth in 80 days would be about 1 / 80 v or 12.5 mv, which is a typical speed for a bicycle. If we flew in a “[pedal powered airship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship#:~:text=pedal%20powered%20airship)” from Cambridge MA to Cambridge UK at an average speed of 12.5 mv, we could complete the journey in ten days: 12500 kz / 12.5 mv = 1000 cd.

At sunrise, the [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} is the amount of time until sunset. At solar noon, the time remaining before sunset will be [da/2](#da2){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="half day arc"}. Throughout the day, the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is equal to the sum of sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the difference between the current and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}: ${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} -- ${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}.


Like a countdown sequence, we can keep track of the time relative to sunset throughout the day. can keep track of the remaining time until sunset by minuend The [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} of sunrise is found by subtracting half the [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} from solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. The [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} of sunset is found by adding half the [da](#da){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day arc"} to solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.

# Sunrise and sunset {#sec-sas .hiddenheading}

## Solar hour angle {#sec-sha .unnumbered .hiddenheading}


To find the UTC [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} of a given longitude and latitude, we could use an [application programming interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20software%20interface%2C%20offering%20a%20service%20to%20other%20pieces%20of%20software) (API) or a [database](https://observablehq.com/@jcolot/time-zone-service). If we only have longitude, we need to first round degrees to zero or the nearest multiple of fifteen for whole hour [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, 7.5 for half hour [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, or 3.75 for quarter hour [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} and then divide by fifteen to convert degrees to hours.

# Next {#next .unnumbered}

The next article in the [Dec section](/dec) of my [site](/) shows how we can combine [Dec dates](/dec/date) and times into [Dec snaps](/dec/snap)🫰, which are analogous to the [combined date and time representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Combined_date_and_time_representations) in the [ISO 8601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#:~:text=an%20international%20standard%20covering%20the%20worldwide%20exchange%20and%20communication%20of%20date%20and%20time%2Drelated%20data) international standard for dates and times. The final article in the Dec section demonstrates how Dec dates, times, and snaps🫰can be paired up to express [time intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Time_intervals:~:text=the%20intervening%20time%20between%20two%20time%20points) called Dec [spans](/dec/span)🌈.
